title: No Top, No Bottom
hook: Brahma and Vishnu are arguing about which of them is greater when a pillar of fire splits the sky between them
carry: the linga: a sign of the God beyond measure
tomorrow: what happens when a father shuts Shiva out?

segments.voice: Yesterday: work offered to God becomes worship, and the goddess's part of the year closed. Today the year turns to Shiva.

Two gods are arguing. Brahma, the creator, says he's the greatest, since everything came from him. Vishnu, the preserver, says no, he is, since he keeps everything going. The argument gets hot. Then, between the two of them, a pillar of fire appears, blazing, going up past where they can see and down past where they can see. No top in sight, and no bottom. Both gods stop mid-sentence. You heard this on Shivaratri, back on day ninety; today it comes from the Shiva Purana itself.
screen: `TWO GODS ARGUING.` → `A PILLAR OF FIRE.` → `NO TOP, NO BOTTOM.`

segments.voice: The Shiva Purana is a big book of Shiva's stories, told aloud by a storyteller named Suta to a gathering of sages; the path takes selections. The two gods agree on a test: whoever finds the end of this thing wins. Vishnu becomes a boar and digs down. Brahma becomes a swan and flies up. Vishnu finds no bottom, and finally comes back and says so. Brahma finds no top. But on the way he meets a ketaki flower drifting down, and he has an idea. He comes back, says he reached the top, and brings the flower along to swear it's true. Then the pillar opens and Shiva steps out of it. He honors Vishnu for telling the truth and rebukes Brahma for the lie, and in the story the ketaki flower, the false witness, is not to be offered in Shiva's worship. Linga means a mark, a sign. For Shaiva devotees, the linga in a Shiva temple recalls this pillar, and that's why the main image in so many Shiva temples has no face and no arms: it's a sign of what can't be measured, God with no top and no bottom, beyond every form. Temple walls carve the moment, Shiva stepping out of the pillar, the boar below, the swan above; it's called Lingodbhava. And the one who comes out well is the one who admitted it: I couldn't find the end. Before God that big, the story honors the honest answer.
screen: `A BOOK OF SHIVA'S STORIES.` · `A BOAR DIGS, A SWAN FLIES.` · `ONE ADMITS IT, ONE LIES.` · `LINGA: A SIGN OF THE UNMEASURED.` · then, large: `NO TOP. NO BOTTOM.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one big question you have no answer to and let it stand in front of you like the pillar, too big to measure. Let any quick answer drift by, like the flower. Then do what devotees do at a Shiva temple, in your mind or with a cup of water at the sink: pour a little water, slowly, as if over the linga. If you pray, say Om Namah Shivaya, bowing to Shiva, or the name of God you use. If you don't, let the water run and say: I don't know the end of this, and that's honest.
The Shiva Purana: Shiva's stories, told by Suta to the sages.
Your line: the linga, a sign of the God beyond measure. Nobody found the end, and the honest one said so. I'll be here tomorrow.

howItsDone: Shaiva Hindus worship Shiva in the form of the linga in temples and homes, and the story of the endless pillar of fire is told and carved in temples as the appearance of the linga, Lingodbhava; it is also linked to Maha Shivaratri.
